assignments.brief_reason: Dislikes cursing mainly due to audience/children exposure, but the rationale is still an exception-based removal of profane/toxic language rather than a threat/violence justification.
Describes moderating direct attacks while reviewing profanity without automatic removal—reflects removing toxicity/threats with a lower bar for non-toxic profanity.
Explicitly accepts harsh language unless it includes threats/calls for violence; aligns with violence/threat exception framing.
States removing hateful and violent language while keeping expression—fits toxicity/threat removal rule.
Uses a disinformation threshold for divergence from free-speech acceptance; this is not captured by the threat/toxicity or same-criteria pair-mirroring themes.
Removal decision driven by offensiveness/uncivil behavior (name-calling), consistent with removing toxic/inflammatory content.
Avoids platforming extreme positions; not clearly tied to threats/violence/toxicity removal criteria in the codebook.
Freedom of expression is accepted unless it harms others—closest to violence/threat exception logic.
Explicitly uses a pair/mirror strategy preference for discussion over provocation; none of the listed themes match this pair-strategy claim.
Personal attacks cause refusal while criticism is acceptable; personal attacks align with removing toxic/inflammatory behavior.
Combines fact-verification attempts with a civility/mean-ness removal reason; does not clearly match the threat/toxicity-only or free-speech-exception themes.
Professionalism/fact-based writing influences keep decisions; not covered by threat/toxicity or same-standard pair criteria.
Kept for constructive discussion; removed for name-calling/purposefully inflammatory or not adding—matches removing inflammatory/toxic content.
Focuses on calibrating intensity/out-of-proportion across the pair; not the same-criteria fairness theme and not a threat/toxicity exception claim.
Allows only if not too aggressive/vulgar and not verbal attacking; reflects removing toxic/incendiary language.
Removes when political alignment sounds extremely right/too influential/appropriate; not clearly anchored to threats/violence/toxicity exceptions.
Removal cue is offensive/incendiary language; many others seem fine—fits removing toxicity/inflammatory language.
Criterion contrasts factual claims vs whining/crying; this is neither threat/violence exception nor profanity/toxicity removal per the definitions.
First Amendment justification with focus on absence of harm toward someone—aligns with keeping most speech unless harm/threat concerns arise.
Bad/profane language strongly drives evaluation; best fit is toxicity removal behavior (though it’s stated as pair-driver, not explicitly threats).
